name: Saint Andrew
blurb: The fisherman, Peter's brother, and patron of Scotland.
story: Andrew brought Peter to Jesus. An X-shaped cross carries his name, and the Scottish flag shows it.
food: Cullen skink, a Scottish smoked fish soup
A Scottish supper of mashed turnips and potatoes
do: Pipe a saltire, his X-shaped cross, on shortbread
Start the St. Andrew Christmas novena
Bring a friend to Mass

name: First Sunday of Advent
blurb: The Church's new year begins and the wait for Christmas starts.
story: Advent looks two ways at once: back to the first Christmas and ahead to Christ's return. It is a quiet, hopeful season that gets its own space before the Christmas parties begin.
food: A simple soup supper while the first candle is lit
do: Start a Jesse Tree
Set up the Advent wreath and light the first purple candle
Hang the Advent calendar
Add decorations a little at a time instead of all at once
Stir up the Christmas baking, an old English custom
Draw a family patron saint for the year from a hat
Add a piece of straw to the manger for each good deed

name: Saint Nicholas
blurb: The bishop who secretly gave gifts, and the real Santa.
story: Nicholas tossed bags of gold through a window to keep three poor girls from being sold, and shoes are still set out the night before.
do: Slip a coin into someone’s shoe, as he did for three poor daughters
Put out shoes the night before
Secretly do something kind
Write letters to Santa

name: Saint Ambrose
blurb: Milan's bishop, patron of beekeepers, who baptized Augustine.
story: Ambrose was a governor, not even baptized, when the crowd in Milan demanded him for bishop. Legend says bees settled on his lips as a baby, a sign of his sweet words.
do: Make a beeswax candle

name: The Immaculate Conception
blurb: Mary is conceived without sin, and it's the U.S. patronal feast.
story: This is about Mary's conception, not Jesus'. Pius IX defined it in 1854, and four years later Mary used the phrase to Bernadette.
do: Light candles in the windows the night before, as Colombian families do
Throw a white party
Go to Mass with the kids
Walk through the house in a little procession for Mary
prayers: A prayer to the Immaculate Conception

name: Saint Juan Diego
blurb: The Mexican peasant who met Our Lady at Tepeyac.
story: An Indigenous farmer on his way to Mass, Juan Diego met Mary at Tepeyac hill and carried her message to a doubtful bishop.
do: Draw roses on a poster-board cloak and act out the story

name: Our Lady of Guadalupe
blurb: Mary appears in Mexico in 1531 and leaves her image on a cloak.
story: Roses in December tumbled out of Juan Diego's cloak in front of the bishop, and her image stayed on it. Patroness of the Americas.
do: Wake up early and sing Las Mañanitas
Bring roses to church
Go to a mariachi Mass
Try braids with ribbons
prayers: St. John Paul II's Prayer to Our Lady of Guadalupe

name: Our Lady of Loreto
blurb: The Marian shrine in Italy, and patroness of pilots.
story: Tradition says the house where Mary grew up was carried to Loreto, Italy, which is how she became patroness of pilots and air travel.
do: Build a gingerbread house, in honor of the Holy House

name: Saint Lucy
blurb: A young martyr whose name means light, near the darkest days of the year.
story: In Sweden, a daughter dresses in a white gown with a red sash and a candle crown, and brings buns to the family before dawn.
food: Cuccìa, the sweet wheat berry dish of Sicily
do: Have the oldest daughter serve breakfast in a candle crown, Swedish style
Winter Ember Days: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after today
Make a paper candle crown
Serve breakfast in bed
Light the Christmas lights tonight

name: Saint John of the Cross
blurb: A Spanish Carmelite mystic.
story: John worked with St. Teresa of Avila to reform the Carmelites and was jailed by his own brothers, writing some of his greatest poetry in that cell.
do: Read a few lines of his poetry aloud
prayers: A passage of The Spiritual Canticle

name: Gaudete Sunday
blurb: The rose candle is lit, and the Church says rejoice because Christmas is close.
story: Gaudete is Latin for rejoice. Halfway through Advent the purple lightens to rose, a small reminder that the waiting has a happy end.
food: Something pink for dessert, like strawberry cake or pink frosted cookies
do: Light the rose candle
Bake something to give to a neighbor
Wear pink
Set up the Nativity scene and have the Baby Jesus figure blessed

name: Christmas
blurb: The birth of Jesus.
story: The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, and the whole season that follows runs to the Baptism of the Lord.
food: Tamales, as many Mexican families do
do: Sing a carol in another language
Sing to Jesus at the manger
Add Baby Jesus to the nativity
Go to Mass as a family
Have a joyful and unhurried day
indulgence: Plenary for devoutly receiving the Pope's Urbi et Orbi blessing, even by television or radio.

name: Saint Stephen
blurb: The first martyr, the day after Christmas.
story: A deacon who served Jerusalem's widows, Stephen forgave the crowd stoning him. Good King Wenceslas went out on the Feast of Stephen.
food: Soups or stews shared with neighbors
do: Go door to door with holly and carols, as Ireland’s wren boys still do
Give a Christmas gift away to someone in need
Sing Good King Wenceslas
Deliver boxes of Christmas cookies to the neighbors, in the spirit of Boxing Day

name: Saint John the Apostle
blurb: The Beloved Disciple.
story: Legend says John drank poisoned wine and lived, so wine is blessed today.
food: Something deep-fried, because legend says he survived a vat of boiling oil
do: Toast each other
Read a bit of John's Gospel

name: The Holy Innocents
blurb: Bethlehem's baby boys, killed by Herod.
story: A heavy feast placed right in the joy of Christmas. An old custom turns the day over to the youngest child.
food: Let the youngest pick the menu
Cream of wheat or grits, as a baby food joke
do: Pray for children who are suffering
Let the baby of the family be in charge
Pray for children in danger
Put the kids in charge for the day
Play harmless pranks

name: The Holy Family
blurb: Jesus, Mary and Joseph as a family, in the days just after Christmas.
story: God chose to grow up in an ordinary home, with parents, chores and a trade to learn. This feast is a good excuse to enjoy your own family.
food: A favorite family recipe, or one handed down from a grandparent
do: Take a family photo
Pray together for each person at the table
Go on a family outing

name: Mary, the Holy Mother of God
blurb: The new year opens with Mary, on the Octave Day of Christmas.
story: Calling Mary Mother of God is really a statement about Jesus: that he is truly God. The Council of Ephesus settled the title in 431.
food: Black-eyed peas and greens, a Southern New Year dish
Twelve grapes at midnight, the Spanish custom
Grapes for good luck, an old Spanish custom
do: Pray together for the new year
Pick a patron saint for the year by drawing names
indulgence: Plenary when the Veni Creator is prayed on January 1. The Te Deum, prayed publicly on December 31, carries one as well.

name: The Most Holy Name of Jesus
blurb: A day to honor the name of Jesus, given at his circumcision.
story: Eight days after his birth, the child received the name the angel had given him. It means God saves.
do: Talk about how we use God's name

name: Saint Elizabeth Ann Seton
blurb: A New York widow and convert who founded Catholic schools, the first American-born saint.
story: Elizabeth Seton raised five children on her own after her husband died, joined the Church over her family's objections, and began the Sisters of Charity in Maryland. Her schools became a model for American Catholic education.
food: New York-style pizza, for her hometown
do: Thank a teacher
Write a note to a Catholic school

name: Saint John Neumann
blurb: Philadelphia's immigrant bishop, who organized a diocesan school system.
story: A Bohemian immigrant, Neumann became Bishop of Philadelphia and built the first diocesan Catholic school system in the country.
do: Thank someone who runs a Catholic school

name: The Epiphany of the Lord
blurb: The Wise Men reach Bethlehem and Christ is shown to all nations.
story: Following a star, foreigners arrive with gold, frankincense and myrrh. Many Catholic homes mark the new year on this day by blessing the house with chalk over the door.
food: Rosca de Reyes, with a tiny baby figure baked inside
King cake with a hidden bean or tiny figure, easy to make from canned cinnamon roll dough in a bundt pan
do: Whoever finds the baby in the rosca hosts tamales at Candlemas
Chalk the door with the year and the initials C, M and B
Crown whoever finds the bean as the family's King or Queen
Let the Wise Men finally reach the nativity scene
Put out shoes overnight for the Wise Men

name: The Baptism of the Lord
blurb: Jesus is baptized in the Jordan, and the Christmas season ends.
story: John hesitates, Jesus insists, and the voice from heaven names him the beloved Son. It is the natural day to remember your own baptisms.
food: A special dessert for anyone with a baptism story to tell
do: Look up everyone’s baptism date and light their baptism candles
Light baptism candles and renew your baptismal promises
Look up each person's baptism date and write it on the calendar

name: Saint Sebastian
blurb: Roman soldier and martyr, shot with arrows, patron of athletes.
story: Sebastian served in the Roman guard while quietly helping Christians. Survived being shot with arrows, then was martyred on confronting the emperor. Patron of athletes and soldiers.
food: Shish kebabs, skewers standing in for the arrows
do: Pray for family athletes and those in the military
Have the team over

name: Saint Agnes
blurb: A young Roman martyr whose name sounds like agnus, the Latin for lamb.
story: Agnes refused to give up her faith as a young girl in third-century Rome. Lambs blessed on her feast still provide wool for the pallium worn by archbishops.
do: Look up the two lambs blessed in Rome today, whose wool becomes the archbishops’ palliums
Learn the story of the blessed lambs in Rome

name: Day of Prayer for the Unborn
blurb: A day of prayer and penance in the U.S. for the legal protection of unborn children.
story: U.S. dioceses keep this day each January, near the anniversary of Roe v. Wade, with prayer and penance. It moves to January 23 if the 22nd is a Sunday.
food: Simple meatless meals as a family offering
do: Pray for a family expecting a baby
Pray for mothers and babies
Bring diapers or supplies to a pregnancy center

name: Saint Vincent of Saragossa
blurb: A Spanish deacon and martyr, patron of winemakers.
story: Vincent was a deacon of Spain tortured under Diocletian. Vineyard country took him as patron, maybe because Vincent sounds like the French for wine.
food: Boeuf bourguignon, from the vineyards that claim him
Grape juice or wine at dinner, and maybe some grapes and cheese
do: Toast the winemakers with grape juice
Sit down and take it easy for an evening
Host a grape juice or wine tasting

name: The Conversion of Saint Paul
blurb: A persecutor of Christians meets Jesus on the road to Damascus.
story: Saul set off to arrest Christians and arrived blind and changed. Paul's letters shaped the Church from then on.
food: A regular family dinner with a good conversation
Hummus and falafel, in honor of Damascus
do: Talk about a time someone surprised you by changing
Play blind man's bluff

name: Saint Thomas Aquinas
blurb: The great Dominican teacher who proved faith and reason are friends.
story: Classmates called him the Dumb Ox because he was big and quiet. His teacher predicted the world would hear that ox bellow, and his Summa still shapes Catholic thought.
food: Big hearty ox-tail or beef stew
do: Ask the hardest question you can think of and try to answer it together
Pray for students

name: Saint Brigid of Ireland
blurb: Ireland's beloved abbess, known for generosity.
story: Stories about Brigid are full of bread, butter and beer that never ran out because she gave everything away. Rush crosses made on her day are still hung over Irish doors.
food: Irish scones or soda bread with butter
do: Leave a cloth outside overnight for her blessing, an Irish custom
Weave a St. Brigid's cross out of straw or paper
Give something away
Shake cream in a jar until it turns to butter

name: Candlemas
blurb: Forty days after Christmas, Jesus is presented in the Temple.
story: Simeon calls the baby a light for the nations, so candles are blessed today for the year ahead. It's also the traditional end of the Christmas decorations and the origin of Groundhog Day's weather lore.
food: Tamales and atole, the Mexican Candelaria meal
Crepes, round and golden like the sun
do: Bring your candles to Mass to be blessed
Eat dinner by candlelight, or leave the electric lights off all day
Take down the last of the Christmas decorations

name: Saint Blaise
blurb: Patron of throat ailments, who saved a boy choking on a fish bone.
story: Blaise was an Armenian bishop and doctor. Priests bless throats on his feast using two candles tied in a cross.
food: A slice of saved Christmas panettone, Milan's custom for healthy throats
Whole fish, and practice finding the bones
do: Get your throat blessed at Mass
Go to Mass for the blessing of throats

name: Saint Agatha
blurb: A Sicilian martyr and patron of Catania, invoked against fire.
story: Agatha is one of the virgin martyrs named at Mass in the Roman Canon. Sicilians honor her with small round cream-filled cakes.
food: Cream puffs or minne di Sant'Agata, round Sicilian cakes
do: Pray for someone facing breast cancer
Pray for women facing illness
Learn where the fire extinguisher is

name: Saint Paul Miki and Companions
blurb: Japanese Catholics and missionaries crucified at Nagasaki in 1597.
story: Paul Miki, a Japanese Jesuit, preached from his cross. Secret Christians kept the faith there for over two hundred years without priests.
food: Sushi, teriyaki or another Japanese meal
do: Fold origami cranes
Pray for Christians who are persecuted today

name: Saint Josephine Bakhita
blurb: Born in Sudan and enslaved as a child, she became a gentle Italian nun.
story: Kidnapped so young that she forgot her own name, Bakhita was later freed in Italy, entered religious life, and was known for her kindness. She is the patron of survivors of trafficking.
food: Italian food, in honor of her adopted home
do: Pray for victims of human trafficking and look up a group that helps them

name: Our Lady of Lourdes
blurb: Mary appears to Bernadette at a French grotto in 1858.
story: Bernadette, a poor and sickly teenager, saw a lady who asked her to dig for a spring. Pilgrims still go to Lourdes for its waters and healing, and it's now World Day of the Sick.
do: Pray for someone who is sick
Visit a local shrine or grotto
Pray for someone who's sick
Make a small family pilgrimage

name: Saints Cyril and Methodius
blurb: Brothers who brought the Gospel and an alphabet to the Slavs.
story: Two brothers from Thessalonica went to the Slavic peoples, created an alphabet, and translated the liturgy into their language.
do: Learn a few letters of the Cyrillic alphabet

name: Saint Valentine
blurb: A third-century martyr who gave his name to a day for love.
story: Little is known about Valentine except that he was a Roman martyr buried on the Flaminian Way, and medieval poets linked his day with love.
do: Slip anonymous valentines around the house
Make valentines for family and for someone lonely
Talk about what real love looks like
Turn the kitchen into a family bistro for the night

name: The Chair of Saint Peter
blurb: A celebration of the pope's teaching office, begun with Peter.
story: The chair stands for the authority to teach. Rome has a real one, encased in bronze by Bernini at the back of St. Peter's.
food: Cookies or candy built into little chairs
do: Write a letter to the Pope
Pray for him by name

name: Saints Perpetua and Felicity
blurb: A young mother and a slave who died together as friends in Carthage.
story: Perpetua kept a prison diary, one of the oldest writings by a Christian woman. She paused in the arena to fix her hair, because she'd go to her death joyfully.
do: Try fancy hairdos
Pray for mothers and new moms
prayers: The Passion of Saints Perpetua and Felicity

name: Saint Frances of Rome
blurb: A wife and mother who served Rome's poor, and is patron of drivers.
story: Frances ran a household, nursed plague victims, and founded a community for lay women. She saw her guardian angel for years, which is why she's patron of drivers.
food: Teach a child to cook a simple recipe
do: Have the car blessed; she watches over drivers
Have everyone learn one home skill
Bless the car

name: Mardi Gras
blurb: Fat Tuesday, the last big party before Lent begins.
story: Before freezers, the rich foods had to be used up before the Lenten fast, which is how pancake suppers and carnival began. The joy of the feast makes the fast mean more.
food: Use up the sweets in the house
do: Run a pancake race, as Olney, England has for centuries
Put on masks and beads
Write Alleluia on a sign or rock and get ready to bury it until Easter
Decide together what each person will do for Lent
Crown a King or Queen of Mardi Gras

name: Ash Wednesday
blurb: Lent begins with ashes, fasting and a reminder of what really matters.
story: Ashes on the forehead recall that life is short and God's mercy is long. Lent's forty days echo Jesus' time in the desert.
food: Capirotada, the Mexican Lenten bread pudding
Soft pretzels, shaped like arms crossed in prayer
A plain meatless supper such as soup and bread
do: Spring Ember Days: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after today
Bury the Alleluia
Set out a jar and start sacrifice beans, one for each kindness or sacrifice, to swap for jelly beans at Easter
Put away the extras and pick a simple Lenten practice

name: Saint Patrick
blurb: The former slave who brought the faith back to Ireland.
story: Kidnapped from Britain as a teenager, Patrick escaped, became a priest and returned to the people who had enslaved him. The shamrock is his simple picture of the Trinity.
do: Throw a Hooley with singing and dancing
Build a leprechaun trap and leave chocolate coins
Pray St. Patrick's Breastplate
Use a shamrock to explain the Trinity

name: Saint Joseph
blurb: Husband of Mary, foster father of Jesus, and patron of the universal Church.
story: Joseph never says a word in the Gospels and does exactly what's needed. In Sicily, a famine answered by his intercession gave rise to St. Joseph's Tables of food shared with the poor.
food: Fava beans, the lucky food of St. Joseph’s Table
Pasta with toasted breadcrumbs for carpenter’s sawdust
Eat with your hands, the Italian way, for fun
do: Build a small St. Joseph’s Table with lilies and tool-shaped breads, then share it with people in need
Set up a St. Joseph's Table of food to share
Do some woodworking or fix something
Pray for fathers and workers
prayers: Begin the Seven Sundays of St. Joseph beforehand

name: The Annunciation
blurb: Gabriel visits Mary, and God becomes man, nine months before Christmas.
story: Mary's yes is the hinge of history. It's a Solemnity in Lent, so the party's on.
food: Fried cod with garlic sauce, the Greek dish for this day
Waffles for dinner, from an old Swedish pun on Lady Day
do: Pray the Angelus at noon
Decorate like a baby announcement, and put on a puppet show

name: Laetare Sunday
blurb: Rejoice, Easter is getting closer, and the violet lightens to rose.
story: Laetare means rejoice. In England it became Mothering Sunday, when people visited their mother church and their mothers.
food: Simnel cake, the traditional Mothering Sunday cake
Simnel cake or anything a little more festive than usual Lenten fare
do: Bring flowers to your mother
Bring flowers to your mother or grandmother
Take a breather and enjoy Sunday
Wear pink

name: Passion Sunday
blurb: The last Sunday before Holy Week, once marked by veiling statues and crosses.
story: Older calendars began Passiontide today, covering statues and crosses in church until Easter.
food: Carlin peas, a Northern England custom for this Sunday
A purple dinner with beets, cabbage or grape juice
do: Veil the statues and crosses at home
Go to confession before Holy Week

name: Palm Sunday
blurb: Jesus enters Jerusalem to shouts of welcome, and Holy Week begins.
story: The same crowds who wave branches will soon turn away. Blessed palms are kept at home through the year, often tucked behind a crucifix.
food: A simple meal, with the Holy Week spring cleaning starting after
do: Weave palm crosses, and save the palms to burn for next year’s ashes
Weave the blessed palms into crosses
Tuck palm behind the crucifixes at home
Clean the house together this week to get ready for Easter

name: Holy Thursday
blurb: The Last Supper, the first Eucharist and the washing of the feet.
story: Jesus gives the Eucharist and kneels to wash his friends' feet. After the evening Mass the bells go quiet until the Easter Vigil.
food: Green foods like herb soup and spinach, for Germany’s Green Thursday
A simple Last Supper meal of lamb, flatbread, herbs and grape juice
A lamb cake made from crispy rice treats
do: Visit several churches after Mass to pray, a custom linked to St. Philip Neri
Wash each other's feet at home
Keep the house quiet from tonight on
Watch The Prince of Egypt
indulgence: Plenary when the Tantum Ergo is prayed solemnly today.

name: Good Friday
blurb: The Lord's Passion and death, kept with fasting and quiet.
story: The one day of the year with no Mass at all. Many families keep the noon to three o'clock hours as quietly as they can.
do: Pray the Stations of the Cross at home with fourteen small crosses
Go without screens and music
Keep three o'clock as a moment of silence
Wear black
Start the Divine Mercy Novena
indulgence: Plenary for taking part in the Adoration of the Cross at the Good Friday liturgy. On any Friday of Lent, the Prayer before a Crucifix after Communion is also plenary.

name: Holy Saturday
blurb: The quiet day of waiting at the tomb, ending at the Easter Vigil.
story: The Church waits without any celebrations until darkness falls and the new fire is lit at the Vigil.
food: A Polish Święconka basket of bread, eggs, ham, salt and horseradish
Prepare a basket of Easter foods to be blessed
do: Take your Easter food to church to be blessed
Dye the eggs
Fill the Easter baskets
Set out the Easter clothes

name: Easter Sunday
blurb: Christ is risen! The greatest day of the Christian year.
story: The empty tomb is the center of the faith, and the party lasts for eight days and then fifty. Alleluia comes back.
food: A butter lamb, the Polish table centerpiece
Hot cross buns and all the sweets you gave up
Shrimp and ham, celebrating every food the new covenant allows
do: Dig up the Alleluia
Trade sacrifice beans for jelly beans
Have an egg hunt
Greet each other with Christ is risen and answer He is risen indeed
Invite someone who would otherwise be alone
indulgence: Plenary for devoutly receiving the Pope's Urbi et Orbi blessing, even by television or radio.

name: Easter Monday
blurb: Easter keeps going, with the Octave's second day.
story: In Poland it's Wet Monday, when people splash each other with water, a playful reminder of baptism.
do: Splash each other with water for Dyngus Day, the Polish custom
Have a picnic, as Italians do for Pasquetta
Have a water fight, or at least a very small splash

name: Easter Tuesday
blurb: Day three of the eight-day Easter celebration.
do: Greet each other with He is risen, and answer He is risen indeed
Pray the Regina Caeli

name: Easter Wednesday
blurb: Still Easter, with the Octave rolling on.
do: Greet each other with He is risen, and answer He is risen indeed
Pray the Regina Caeli

name: Easter Thursday
blurb: Still Easter, one more day of feasting.
do: Greet each other with He is risen, and answer He is risen indeed
Pray the Regina Caeli

name: Easter Friday
blurb: A Friday without penance, because Easter outranks it.
story: Every day of the Easter Octave counts as a solemnity, so meat is back on the table on the one Friday when it's easy to forget.
food: Burgers or steak, because it's a meat Friday

name: Easter Saturday
blurb: The last weekday of the Easter Octave.
do: Greet each other with He is risen, and answer He is risen indeed
Pray the Regina Caeli

name: Divine Mercy Sunday
blurb: The Sunday after Easter, on God's mercy, as revealed to St. Faustina.
story: St. Faustina Kowalska's visions of Christ led St. John Paul II to name this Sunday in 2000. Many parishes offer the Chaplet at three in the afternoon.
do: Pray the Divine Mercy Chaplet at three
Go to confession around this time
indulgence: Plenary for taking part in Divine Mercy devotions in a church, or for praying the Our Father, the Creed and a prayer such as “Merciful Jesus, I trust in you!” before the Blessed Sacrament.

name: Saint George
blurb: The soldier-martyr of the dragon story and patron of England.
story: Almost nothing is known about the real George except that he died for the faith. The dragon story stuck because everyone understands what it is to fight a monster.
food: A fruit crumble marked with a St. George's Cross
do: Give someone a rose and a book, as Catalonia does for Sant Jordi
Dress as knights and ladies
Have a dragon hunt
Talk about what dragons you'd like to slay
Stage cardboard sword fights

name: Saint Mark
blurb: Writer of the shortest Gospel, symbolized by a lion.
story: Tradition makes Mark the companion of Peter and founder of the Church in Alexandria. Venice has claimed him since his relics arrived in the 800s.
food: Risi e bisi, the rice and peas of Venice
Venetian rice and peas, risi e bisi
do: Give someone a rosebud, a Venetian custom for this day
Read a chapter of Mark's Gospel out loud
Draw a winged lion
Walk the neighborhood and pray for the people who live there, an old Rogation custom

name: Saint Gianna Molla
blurb: An Italian doctor and mother who gave her life for her unborn child.
story: Gianna was a pediatrician, wife and mother who loved skiing and fashion. She chose treatment that protected her baby and died a week after her daughter's birth.
do: Pray for mothers and doctors
Give the moms a night out

name: Saint Catherine of Siena
blurb: A wool-dyer's daughter who told popes what to do.
story: The twenty-fourth of twenty-five children, Catherine nursed plague victims, dictated a book, and persuaded the pope to leave Avignon for Rome. She's a Doctor of the Church.
food: Italian food and something lovely for the table
do: Write an honest, loving letter to someone in charge

name: Saint Joseph the Worker
blurb: Honoring work and workers on May Day.
story: Pius XII set this feast in 1955 as a response to communist May Day rallies, naming a carpenter as the model of working people.
do: Do a home project together
Thank someone for their work

name: Our Lady of Fatima
blurb: Mary appears to three shepherd children in Portugal in 1917.
story: Lucia, Francisco and Jacinta were asked to pray the Rosary for peace. Some 70,000 saw the sun appear to dance that October.
food: Pastéis de nata, Portuguese custard tarts
Portuguese sweet bread or custard tarts
Cupcakes decorated like a dancing sun
do: Hold a candlelit rosary walk
Pray the Rosary together
Act out the story

name: Saint Christopher Magallanes and Companions
blurb: Priests and laymen martyred during the Mexican persecution of the 1920s.
story: Mexico's government closed churches in the 1920s and these martyrs kept serving in secret. Father Magallanes forgave his executioners as he died.
do: Pray for persecuted Christians
Watch or read about the Cristero War with older kids
Whack a pinata

name: Saint Rita of Cascia
blurb: Patron of impossible causes, a wife, mother and Augustinian nun.
story: Rita endured a hard marriage and the loss of her family before entering a convent. Baseball fans know her from The Rookie, whose real-life story has a Rita connection.
do: Bring roses to be blessed
Go to a baseball game, or watch The Rookie
Pray for someone in a tough spot

name: Saint Joan of Arc
blurb: The French peasant girl who led an army, patron of France.
story: Joan was still a teenager when she persuaded the Dauphin to let her lead his troops. Burned at nineteen, she was declared a saint centuries later.
do: Learn the story
Make a paper banner

name: The Visitation
blurb: Pregnant Mary visits Elizabeth, and John leaps for joy.
story: The Magnificat is Mary's song of praise on this visit, and she stayed three months to help.
food: Bring a meal to someone expecting
do: Pray the Magnificat
Deliver a casserole to a new or expectant mom

name: The Ascension of the Lord
blurb: Forty days after Easter, Jesus returns to the Father.
story: Jesus blesses his friends, rises out of sight, and tells them to wait for the Spirit. The nine days after were the first novena.
food: Any bird, an old European nod to the day
Popovers, which rise up and are empty inside
do: Begin the Pentecost novena
Fly a kite
Climb a hill and have a picnic

name: Pentecost Sunday
blurb: The Holy Spirit comes in wind and fire, and Easter season ends.
story: Frightened disciples burst out into the streets speaking every language, and the Church goes public.
food: Donuts and hot dogs by the fire
do: Scatter red rose petals, as they do through the roof of Rome’s Pantheon
Summer Ember Days: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after today
Have a backyard bonfire
Wear red
Hang red streamers or paper flames
Pin paper flames on pictures of the Apostles
indulgence: Plenary when the Veni Creator is prayed today.

name: Mary, Mother of the Church
blurb: The day after Pentecost honors Mary as mother of all believers.
story: Pope Francis added this memorial to the calendar in 2018, on the Monday after Pentecost, remembering Mary in the upper room with the first Christians.
food: A homey meal like meatloaf and apple pie
do: Pray a Rosary together

name: The Most Holy Trinity
blurb: One God in three Persons.
story: No analogy quite works, as St. Patrick's shamrock cheerfully shows. The feast celebrates a God who is a relationship of love at his very center.
food: Anything in threes, such as three-meat chili
do: Draw a shamrock or triangle
Pray the Glory Be slowly together

name: Corpus Christi
blurb: The Body and Blood of Christ, honored with processions through the streets.
story: St. Juliana of Liege's devotion and St. Thomas Aquinas' hymns gave this feast its shape, and many towns still carpet streets with flowers.
do: Lay out a flower carpet on the front walk, like Italy’s infiorate
Join a parish Eucharistic procession
Stop in for adoration
Start making the Sign of the Cross when you pass a Catholic church
indulgence: Plenary when the Tantum Ergo is prayed solemnly today.

name: The Most Sacred Heart of Jesus
blurb: A Friday solemnity honoring Jesus' love, so meat is on the menu.
story: St. Margaret Mary Alacoque's visions spread this devotion far and wide. Because it's a solemnity, the usual Friday penance gives way.
do: Enthrone or bless a Sacred Heart image at home
Pray the Litany of the Sacred Heart
prayers: Act of Reparation to the Sacred Heart
indulgence: Plenary when the Act of Reparation is prayed publicly today.

name: The Immaculate Heart of Mary
blurb: The day after the Sacred Heart, honoring Mary's love for God.
story: Mary kept all these things in her heart, Luke tells us. Our Lady of Fatima asked for devotion to her Immaculate Heart.
food: Heart-shaped food, or white food and waffles

name: Saint Anthony of Padua
blurb: The Franciscan preacher who helps find what's lost.
story: Anthony was so gifted a preacher that legend says even the fish came to listen. Tony, Tony, look around is a prayer many Catholic kids know.
food: St. Anthony's bread, baked and shared with the poor
do: Give someone a pot of basil with a little note, Lisbon style
Give bread or money to the poor as St. Anthony’s Bread
Keep a St. Anthony box for lost and found things, and let kids ransom their stuff with a chore or small coin
Pray when something is lost

name: Saints John Fisher and Thomas More
blurb: A bishop and a lawyer who refused to bend to Henry VIII.
story: More was the king's chancellor and a witty family man. He told the crowd he died the king's good servant, but God's first.
food: Fish and s'mores, for Fisher and More
do: Watch or read A Man for All Seasons with older kids
Pray for those in public service

name: The Birth of Saint John the Baptist
blurb: The forerunner's birthday, exactly six months before Christmas.
story: John's birth falls near the summer solstice, as the days begin shrinking, because he must decrease so Christ can increase. The Church has a blessing for St. John's bonfires.
food: Picnic food, with honey and locusts if you're brave
do: Light a bonfire on the eve
Bless the fire
Have a family cookout

name: Saint Josemaria Escriva
blurb: A Spanish priest who taught that ordinary work can be holy.
story: A Spanish priest who founded Opus Dei, he taught that ordinary jobs and family life are a path to holiness.
do: Pick one daily chore and offer it up

name: Saints Peter and Paul
blurb: The two pillars of the Church in Rome.
story: The fisherman and the tentmaker were both martyred in Rome and share a single day. Tradition says Peter was crucified upside down, and Paul was beheaded.
food: Fish for Peter and something woven like braided bread for Paul the tentmaker
do: Visit a cathedral or basilica and pray an Our Father and the Creed
Pray for the Pope
Go camping or fishing
prayers: Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, intercede for us
indulgence: Plenary for using an article of devotion blessed by the Pope or a bishop, with a profession of faith.

name: Saint Kateri Tekakwitha
blurb: The Lily of the Mohawks, first Native American saint.
story: Scarred by smallpox and rejected for converting, Kateri fled to a Christian community near Montreal. Her face was said to clear when she died at 24.
food: Corn soup or succotash, traditional foods of her people
Three sisters stew of corn, beans and squash
do: Take a walk outside and pray
Make a simple cross of sticks

name: Our Lady of Mount Carmel
blurb: Patroness of the Carmelites and of the Brown Scapular.
story: Carmelite tradition says Mary gave the scapular to St. Simon Stock in the 1200s. It's a small sign of being under her care.
food: A brown-and-white dessert like brownies or tiramisu
do: Get enrolled in the scapular
Learn about Mount Carmel

name: Saint Mary Magdalene
blurb: The first witness of the Resurrection, called Apostle to the Apostles.
story: Mary Magdalene stayed at the cross and came to the tomb. An old story has her telling the emperor about the Resurrection, holding up an egg that turned red.
food: A spice-filled meal for the spices she brought to the tomb
do: Dye eggs red
Tell someone good news
Play an egg-tapping game

name: Saint Bridget of Sweden
blurb: A Swedish mother of eight and founder of an order.
story: Bridget raised a big family and advised kings before founding the Bridgettines. One of her daughters, Catherine, also became a saint.
do: Learn a few words of Swedish

name: Saints Joachim and Anne
blurb: Mary's parents, and the patrons of grandparents.
story: Scripture doesn't name them, but early Christian tradition does. Their feast is the perfect day to call the grandparents.
food: Share a meal with a grandparent or elderly neighbor
do: Visit or call a grandparent
Have grandparents tell stories about when they were young

name: The Transfiguration of the Lord
blurb: Jesus shines with glory on the mountain before Peter, James and John.
story: Peter wanted to stay up there forever. It's a preview of what's coming, so in many places grapes and first fruits are blessed today.
food: Grapes and something bright and shining
Toad in the hole, or leftovers transformed into something new
do: Have fruit blessed, an Eastern Christian custom
Talk about what you hope heaven's like
Climb a hill

name: Saint Lawrence
blurb: The deacon of Rome known for grilling humor and care for the poor.
story: Told to bring the Church's treasures, Lawrence brought the poor. Tradition says he joked from the gridiron, which is why he's patron of cooks and comedians.
do: Stay up for the Perseid meteors, nicknamed the Tears of St. Lawrence
Tell jokes at dinner
Go out and watch the Perseid meteors, the Tears of St. Lawrence
Hold a family comedy showcase

name: Saint Clare
blurb: Friend of St. Francis and founder of the Poor Clares, patron of television.
story: Too sick to attend Mass one Christmas, Clare reportedly saw and heard it on her wall, which is why she's the patron of TV.
do: Have a family movie night, honoring her TV patronage
Give away something you don't need

name: The Assumption of Mary
blurb: Mary is taken body and soul into heaven.
story: Blessing herbs today is an old custom in much of Europe, and there's a fragrant story of flowers filling her empty tomb.
food: Grapes, first blessed today in Armenian churches
Herb-roasted chicken and watermelon salad with fresh herbs
do: Bring fruit and herbs to be blessed
Bring herbs and flowers to be blessed
Have a small Marian procession around the yard, singing and ending at a statue
Dry herbs and sew a small sachet

name: The Queenship of Mary
blurb: An octave after the Assumption, Mary is honored as Queen.
story: Pius XII set this memorial in 1954. In the kings of Judah, the queen was the king's mother, which helps explain this title.
food: Queen cakes and coronation chicken sandwiches
do: Crown a statue of Mary with flowers
Have a Marian tea party

name: Saint Bartholomew
blurb: An Apostle often identified with Nathanael, and patron of leatherworkers.
story: Bartholomew reportedly took the Gospel to India and Armenia and was martyred. Tradition says he was skinned alive, so peeled apples are a slightly gruesome family joke.
food: Apple dishes with the skin peeled away
do: Peel an apple all in one piece

name: Saint Monica
blurb: The persistent, praying mother of St. Augustine.
story: Monica prayed for years that Augustine would change. A bishop told her a child of so many tears could not be lost.
food: A good North African dish like couscous
do: Pray for someone who has left the faith
Thank your mom

name: Saint Augustine
blurb: The restless young man who became the great bishop of Hippo.
story: Augustine's Confessions tells of his wandering and conversion. His line about our hearts being restless until they rest in God is still quoted.
food: Pears, for the pears he famously stole
do: Read a page of the Confessions
Own up to something you did wrong
Dig a hole at the beach, after the story of the child he met by the sea
prayers: Holy Spirit Prayer of St. Augustine

name: The Passion of Saint John the Baptist
blurb: John is martyred at Herod's order.
story: Herod had John arrested for speaking the truth, then ordered his death to keep a promise made at a party.
food: A head of lettuce on a platter, and lettuce wraps
do: Act out the story, if your kids can take it

name: Saint Teresa of Calcutta
blurb: Tiny, tireless servant of the poorest of the poor.
story: Mother Teresa left a teaching job to serve the dying in Calcutta's streets, and her Missionaries of Charity now span the world.
food: Or a meal delivered to someone in need
White Jell-O with blue stripes, for her sari
do: Serve at a soup kitchen
Do something small with great love
Pray for the poor and give something to help

name: The Nativity of Mary
blurb: Mary's birthday, nine months after her Immaculate Conception.
story: The Church celebrates only three birthdays: Jesus, Mary, and John the Baptist. A blue cake is right for a queen.
food: A birthday cake with blue frosting
do: Sing Happy Birthday to Mary
Decorate in blue

name: The Exaltation of the Holy Cross
blurb: Honoring the Cross as the sign of victory.
story: St. Helena is said to have found the True Cross in Jerusalem, and this feast recalls the dedication of the church built there.
food: Basil, said to have grown where the Cross was found
do: Take home a sprig of basil, as Greek parishes do
Fall Ember Days: Wednesday, Friday and Saturday after today
Make crosses from sticks and twine
Say a slow Sign of the Cross together

name: Our Lady of Sorrows
blurb: Mary's seven sorrows, the day after the Holy Cross.
story: Simeon told Mary a sword would pierce her heart, and the seven sorrows follow the story through to the tomb.
do: Hand out seven sour candies, and read a verse on each sorrow while sticking a toothpick into a play-dough heart

name: Saint Matthew
blurb: The tax collector who followed Jesus and wrote a Gospel.
story: Jesus called a despised tax man to be an Apostle, and Matthew threw a party to introduce his friends.
food: A big dinner for friends who don't know each other
do: Count coins and give some to the poor
Play a math game

name: Michaelmas
blurb: Saints Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, the archangels.
story: Michael is the warrior who threw out the devil. In old folk tales, the devil fell into a blackberry bramble and cursed it, so people picked blackberries before this day.
food: Struan Micheil, the Scottish St. Michael’s bannock
Deviled eggs and angel food cake
do: Hide a ring in a pie, an old Irish custom
Whack a devil pinata
Pray the St. Michael Prayer

name: Saint Therese of Lisieux
blurb: The Little Flower, who taught the little way of love.
story: She died at 24 in a French convent and her autobiography changed millions of lives. She promised to spend heaven doing good on earth and letting fall a shower of roses.
do: Do small things with great love
Buy or pick roses
Keep a string of sacrifice beads

name: The Guardian Angels
blurb: Each person's angel, sent to guard and guide.
story: Jesus said the little ones have angels who see the Father's face. The Angel of God prayer is one of the first prayers children learn.
do: Pray the Angel of God
Set an extra place at the table for your angel
Say good morning to your guardian angel

name: Saint Francis of Assisi
blurb: The rich young man who gave it all away and loved all creatures.
story: Francis stripped off his fine clothes in the town square and went off to rebuild the Church. His Canticle of the Creatures sings of Brother Sun and Sister Moon.
food: Italian food, and treats for pets
do: Bring pets for a blessing
Go outdoors and enjoy creation
Give away something you love
Build a bird feeder
Visit the zoo

name: Our Lady of the Rosary
blurb: Remembering the Rosary's power, begun after the Battle of Lepanto.
story: St. Pius V credited the 1571 naval victory at Lepanto to Europe's praying of the Rosary.
food: Edible rosaries made from candy on a string, or cereal
do: Pray a family Rosary
Make rosaries from knotted cord

name: Saint Luke
blurb: The physician who wrote a Gospel, and patron of artists and doctors.
story: Luke tells the Christmas story, and tradition says he painted Mary's picture.
do: Paint or draw together
Thank a doctor or nurse
Spend time outside
Visit an art museum

name: Saint John Paul II
blurb: The Polish pope who traveled the world and loved the young.
story: Karol Wojtyla acted, skied and hiked, survived the Nazis and communism, and led the Church for almost 27 years. He later visited and forgave the man who shot him.
do: Take a family walk or hike
Pray for the youth
prayers: St. John Paul II's Act of Entrustment to Mary

name: All Hallows' Eve
blurb: The vigil of All Saints, which gave Halloween its name.
story: Halloween began as the night before All Saints. Spooky and sacred sit side by side, since the saints have conquered the scary stuff.
food: Spooky mac and cheese with food coloring
do: Trick-or-treat and pray for the dead
Carve a pumpkin
Pick out your saint costume for tomorrow

name: All Saints' Day
blurb: Honoring all the saints in heaven, known and unknown.
story: It's the day for every holy person whose name you've never heard, including perhaps a great-grandmother.
food: A feast with something themed for each person's saint
do: Dress as your favorite saint and have the others guess
Throw an All Saints party
Have a saint trivia game
Put on an All Saints pageant
indulgence: Plenary each day from November 1 to 8 for visiting a cemetery and praying for the dead. It applies only to the souls in purgatory.

name: All Souls' Day
blurb: Praying for the dead.
story: Catholics believe we can help those who've died through prayer. Visiting graves in November is a long-standing custom.
food: Pan de muerto, Mexico’s bread for the dead
Pan de muerto, Mexican bread of the dead
do: Set up an ofrenda with photos and favorite foods, Mexican style
Clean a family grave and leave flowers
Visit a cemetery and pray
Write down the names of your dead and pray for them all month
Write the names of loved ones who have died on a candle
Set their photos out on a home altar
indulgence: Plenary, for the souls in purgatory only, for visiting a church today and praying the Our Father and the Creed. Visiting a cemetery counts through November 8.

name: Martinmas
blurb: The soldier who cut his cloak in two for a beggar.
story: In a dream, Martin saw Christ wearing the half of the cloak he had given away. Across Europe children walk with lanterns on his feast.
food: Cookies broken in half and shared
do: Make paper lanterns and walk the neighborhood at dusk
Give a coat to someone who needs one
Donate coats you no longer use

name: Saint Catherine of Alexandria
blurb: A brilliant young martyr, patron of philosophers.
story: Catherine out-argued the emperor's philosophers and the wheel meant to kill her shattered. Pinwheel-shaped Catherine Wheels get their name from her.
do: Learn something hard
Spin a pinwheel
Wear fancy hats

name: Christ the King
blurb: The last Sunday of the Church year crowns Christ as King of all.
story: Pope Pius XI added this feast in 1925 as nationalism was on the rise. It closes the year, and Advent begins the next week.
do: Make paper crowns
Hold a small procession around the house
prayers: Act of Dedication of the Human Race to Christ the King
indulgence: Plenary when the Act of Dedication to Christ the King is prayed publicly today.

name: Holy Monday
blurb: The first quiet days of Holy Week, good for getting the house ready.
story: Monday and Tuesday of Holy Week are a practical pause before the Triduum.
food: A big pot of soup that lasts for days
do: Clean the house together for Easter
Start prepping the Easter food

name: Holy Tuesday
blurb: Another day to clean, cook and get ready for Easter.
story: Jesus spent these days teaching in the Temple while the plot against him came together.
food: More of that big pot of soup
do: Finish a room or two of cleaning

name: Spy Wednesday
blurb: The day Judas agreed to hand Jesus over.
story: The name comes from Judas spying for a chance to betray him, for thirty pieces of silver.
food: Soup and bread by candlelight, blowing out a candle after each reading, like a home Tenebrae
do: Count out thirty silver coins and talk about what Judas traded away

name: Christmas Eve
blurb: The vigil of Christmas, also once the feast of Adam and Eve.
story: Medieval towns staged Paradise plays today around a tree hung with apples, one of the roots of the Christmas tree.
food: The Italian-American Feast of the Seven Fishes
Polish Wigilia, a meatless supper of twelve dishes
A simple meatless supper, keeping the old vigil fast
do: Leave an empty place at the table for the unexpected guest, a Polish custom
Act out Las Posadas, knocking on doors to look for room at the inn
Decorate the Christmas tree
Act out a short Adam and Eve play
Place Baby Jesus in the manger at bedtime

name: Saint Catherine of Sweden
blurb: St. Bridget's daughter, remembered by families who have lost a baby.
story: Catherine of Vadstena led the religious order her mother founded. Families turn to her after miscarriage and stillbirth.
do: Pray for babies lost before birth
Take an older child on a one-on-one outing

name: Our Lady, Queen of Angels
blurb: Mary's title at St. Francis's little chapel, and the namesake of Los Angeles.
story: St. Francis loved a tiny chapel near Assisi called the Portiuncula, dedicated to Our Lady of the Angels. Spanish explorers later carried her name to the river that gave Los Angeles its name.
do: Look up how Los Angeles got its name
Visit a church and pray there
indulgence: Plenary for the Portiuncula: visit your parish church today and pray the Our Father and the Creed. Your bishop may name another day.
